deep.reconstruction:
PART A (continued from the previous page). Let y(x) = sum_{n>=1} x^{n!}/(n!)!. This series converges for every x, so y is entire. CLAIM: y satisfies no algebraic differential equation, i.e. it is 'hypertranscendental' (transcendentally transcendental).

Proof sketch on the page:
(1) Suppose G(x, y, y', ..., y^{(r)}) = 0, where G is a polynomial of total degree s.
(2) Choose n > s and n > r (implicitly: n large enough). Hilbert asserts that each single term a_n x^{n!} of the series must then satisfy H(x, y, ..., y^{(r)}) = 0. Here H is G with its y-free part G_0(x) removed.
(3) Hence H = 0 is satisfied by infinitely many powers x^m. Hilbert concludes that it is satisfied by every power. In a later interlinear insertion he adds: and by every sum of powers, hence by every polynomial.
(4) But H = 0 determines y^{(r)} in terms of the lower derivatives. So one can always write down an analytic function that does not satisfy it, e.g. a polynomial with suitably prescribed values y(x0), ..., y^{(r)}(x0). This is a contradiction.
(5) Added remark, without proof: the same function satisfies no algebraic functional equation.

My reconstruction of step (2), which the page leaves implicit:
- Split G = sum_b G_b, where G_b is the part homogeneous of degree b in the variables (y, y', ..., y^{(r)}).
- Substitute the series. A product of b factors, all taken from the n-th term, gives exponents b*n! + O(rs + s).
- Any product that uses a lower-index term has exponent at most (b-1)n! + s(n-1)! + O(1). Since n > s, s(n-1)! < n!, so this lies well below the window around b*n!.
- Any product that uses a higher-index term has exponent at least (n+1)! - O(1) > s*n!.
- The y-free terms have exponent at most s.
- So the coefficients in the window around b*n! come only from G_b evaluated at the single term. Hence G_b(x, x^{N}, ...) = 0 for N = n!, n large. This is stronger than Hilbert's statement, since H = sum_{b>=1} G_b.
- G_b(x, x^m, ..., (x^m)^{(r)}) = x^{bm} * P_b(x, m), with P_b a Laurent polynomial in x and a polynomial in m. Vanishing for infinitely many m forces P_b to vanish identically in m. So every c*x^m, for every m, satisfies every G_b and hence H.
- Note that the coefficients 1/(n!)! play no role in the argument; they only make the series entire.

PART B. Two claims from algebraic geometry.
(i) Every line complex (an algebraic 3-parameter family of lines in P^3) is given by a single equation in the Plücker coordinates p_ik. In modern terms: every hypersurface of the Klein quadric G(2,4) in P^5 is cut out by one further hypersurface.
(ii) There exist quartic surfaces f_4 = 0 on which every curve is a complete intersection with another surface.

Hilbert begins an indirect proof of (ii). If a curve F = 0 on the quartic were not such a section, there would be a relation A(x)F(x) = phi(x1,x2,x3) psi(x1,x2,x3) chi(x1,x2,x3)... + B(x) f_4(x). The factors phi, psi, chi are cones, i.e. forms in three of the four variables. The continuation on the next page argues via products of linear forms: l m ... F = A phi + B f.
errors: Step (3) has a genuine gap. From 'infinitely many powers x^m satisfy H' one does get that all c*x^m satisfy H, but NOT that sums of powers or polynomials do. Counterexample: H = x*(y*y'' - y'^2) + y*y' = y^2*(x*u)' with u = y'/y. Every c*x^m satisfies H = 0, yet y = x + x^2 gives H = x^2, which is not zero.
Consequently the contradiction in step (4) is not reached as written. A 2-parameter family c*x^m of solutions does not contradict an equation of order r >= 2 that determines y^{(r)}.

The gap is repairable with the same idea. Consider exponent windows near j_1*N_1 + j_2*N_2 + ... for several large factorials N_i = n_i!. These show that the polarizations of each G_b vanish on tuples of distinct powers x^{N_i}. Zariski density of the admissible exponent tuples then gives G_b(sum c_i x^{m_i}) = 0, so H vanishes on all polynomials and step (4) goes through. Hilbert's insertion suggests he sensed the need for this, but his justification 'da ihr unendlich viele Potenzen genügen' is insufficient.

The isolation of single terms (step 2) is asserted without the exponent bookkeeping. It is correct for n sufficiently large, but 'n > s and n > r' is slightly too casual: one also needs (n-1)*(n-1)! > s*(r+1) or similar.
'Dieselbe Funktion genügt keiner algebraischen Funktionalgleichung' is unproven and vague as stated.

Part B(ii) is only begun on this page, and the existence claim is not proved here. The rigorous proof (Noether–Lefschetz) needs transcendental or degeneration methods. The elementary ideal-theoretic approach suggested by the next page is doubtful.

results.what: The entire lacunary series sum x^{n!}/(n!)! satisfies no algebraic differential equation. Method: gap isolation of homogeneous components.
results.modern_name: Hypertranscendence of lacunary power series (gap theorem for D-algebraic / differentially algebraic functions)
results.usually_credited_to: Hölder (1887) for Gamma (first hypertranscendence result); E. H. Moore (1897); Ostrowski (1920s) for Dirichlet series; general gap theorem: Lipshitz & Rubel (1986)

results.what: Every algebraic line complex is defined by a single equation in Plücker coordinates.
results.modern_name: Divisors on the Klein quadric G(2,4) are complete intersections (Pic G(2,4) = Z, projective normality)
results.usually_credited_to: Plücker/Klein (definition of complexes); modern proof via Lefschetz/Grothendieck–Lefschetz

results.what: Existence of quartic surfaces on which every curve is a complete intersection, with the start of an ideal-theoretic proof.
results.modern_name: Noether–Lefschetz theorem (general surface of degree >= 4 in P^3 has Picard group Z·H)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains a private sketch of a hypertranscendence proof for a factorial-gap lacunary series, probably from the 1890s. Its key idea, isolating homogeneous components by gap exponents, anticipates the gap-theorem approach (Ostrowski; Lipshitz–Rubel 1986). The proof as written has a real gap, though it is repairable. The Noether–Lefschetz-type claim is attributed to Noether, and Hilbert's attempt is only begun here. The material is notable as unpublished detail but not a major priority claim.

checkable.asserts: Every power x^m satisfies H = x(yy''-y'^2)+yy' = 0 (result 0).
The sum x+x^2 does NOT satisfy that H (result x**2), refuting 'every sum of powers satisfies H'.
Coefficient ratios tend to 0, consistent with sum x^{n!}/(n!)! being entire.

checkable.sympy: all((n-1)*factorial(n-1) > s*(r+1) for s in range(1,8) for r in range(1,8) for n in range(max(s,r)+3, max(s,r)+6))
checkable.asserts: Exponent windows around b*n! are separated from mixed products once n is somewhat larger than s and r.
A homogeneous component evaluated at c*x^m is c^b x^{bm-k} times a polynomial in m, so vanishing for infinitely many m forces identical vanishing.
